transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because I just seem to worry about everything lately. I mean, everything. Clients, the housing market, my family, money... even just whether moving into my new condo was the right decision. It just feels like it's out of proportion to what's actually happening, you know?
How long have you been experiencing this level of constant worry - has it been going on for months, or did it start more recently around a specific event, like your move?
It's been going on for a while now... I'd say about a year and two months. It really started right after I sold my longtime house and made the move into the condo.
Along with the worry, have you noticed physical symptoms like feeling restless or on edge, muscle tension, or getting tired easily?

I definitely notice the muscle tension. By the end of the day, my neck and shoulders just feel really tight, almost like I've been bracing myself. And I actually catch myself clenching my jaw sometimes, usually when I'm driving between listings or just sitting at my desk.
Over this past year, have you noticed a persistent low mood or a loss of interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

No, I wouldn't say that. I don't really feel down or sad. I still enjoy the things I usually like to do, and I still like seeing my friends and all that. It's really just the constant worrying that's the problem, not my mood.

latest_inference.note: Denial of depressed mood/anhedonia rules out F32.9. Chronic (>6 months) diffuse worry with physical symptoms (muscle tension) meets criteria for GAD, making F41.1 most likely and F41.9 (unspecified) no longer needed.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports excessive, difficult-to-control worry about multiple life domains (work, family, finances, health) persisting for approximately 14 months, well beyond the 6-month threshold required for Generalized Anxiety Disorder. Associated somatic symptoms include muscle tension and jaw clenching, consistent with GAD's physiological criteria. No depressive symptoms (low mood, anhedonia) are present, arguing against a depressive or mixed anxiety-depressive disorder. While symptom onset correlates with a life transition (selling home, moving to condo), the worry has generalized beyond that single stressor and persisted well past the typical adjustment disorder duration, making Adjustment Disorder less likely. The chronicity, breadth of worry domains, and somatic tension symptoms best fit Generalized Anxiety Disorder.
